title: Assistive Access on iPhone: A Simpler Phone Without Buying a Simple Phone
subtitle: Apple's free, built-in Assistive Access mode trims an iPhone down to big buttons and a few chosen apps; here is what it does, what it leaves out, and which phones to set it up on.
excerpt: Assistive Access is a free mode built into the iPhone that shows only big buttons and the apps you choose. Here is how it works, its important limits, and what an iPhone 17 or iPhone 16 costs.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A modern smartphone can do almost anything, and that is exactly the trouble for some people. Rows of tiny icons, pop-up alerts and swipes that open the wrong screen can turn a simple phone call into a frustrating puzzle.

Families often wonder whether they need a special phone for a parent who finds the iPhone confusing. If the person already has an iPhone, or the family uses iPhones, there may be a simpler answer hiding in the Settings app. It is called Assistive Access, and it costs nothing extra.

A quick note on where this information comes from: it is drawn from Apple's own store and support pages, not from independent reviews, and the author has not tested these phones or the mode. Please treat it as a starting point, not a verdict. This guide covers iPhones only; Android equivalents were not researched, so households that need Android should look elsewhere.

Assistive Access is a mode built into the iPhone's software. When it is turned on, the busy home screen goes away. In its place, the person sees a short list of large buttons for only the apps a family member or caregiver has picked.

Apple redesigned the core apps for this mode, including calls, messages, the camera and music. The mode also includes an emoji-only keyboard and video-selfie messaging. Items are bigger, and there are fewer features to sort through.

One honest note: Apple describes Assistive Access as designed for people with cognitive disabilities. Some families may consider it for an older relative who simply finds the phone overwhelming, or who has trouble seeing or hearing. Whether it is a good fit in those cases is a judgment call, and the research behind this guide does not confirm how well it suits those users. For hearing or vision concerns, ask the person's doctor or audiologist, and try the mode together before deciding.
A simpler phone also means some things work differently, and a few of them matter for safety.

items: Emergency calls: the person can still reach emergency services through an Emergency keypad, but automatic emergency dialing is not available inside the mode. Crash Detection keeps working.
Satellite SOS: it only works after leaving the mode.
Who they can reach: unless the supporter allows calls with anyone, the person can only call or message approved contacts.
Updates: installing software updates and changing app permissions both require leaving the mode, and the mode does not show a notice when an update is ready.
Status icons: network, Airplane Mode, Focus and Bluetooth status are hidden inside the mode.

sections.content: "Emergency SOS via satellite isn't available in Assistive Access" — Apple Support

Assistive Access is not a monitored medical alert service. Nobody is watching on the other end, and that is a real limit. If your relative needs round-the-clock help, talk with their doctor about other options. In an emergency, call 911.

items: Check what phone they already have. The mode is free, so an iPhone already in the drawer may be all you need before buying something new.
Budget for the plan, not just the phone. The phones have no monthly fee of their own, but carrier plans are extra, and this guide did not research their costs.
Look at trade-in offers. Apple's pages advertise credit for older iPhones, which can bring the price down.
Confirm the price at checkout. Store prices and offers can change, so check the final total before paying.
Plan who will help. Someone needs to set it up, approve contacts and check for updates from time to time.

sections.content: Setup starts in Settings, then Accessibility, then Assistive Access. The phone walks you through choosing apps and contacts. Have the person's iPhone passcode or Apple Account password handy, because setup may ask for it.

Apple suggests a trusted supporter, such as a family member or caregiver, help with the choices. Sit down together and keep the first version very short: phone, messages, camera, and perhaps photos or music. You can always add more later.

Before turning on Assistive Access, open the Health app and fill in Medical ID with medications, allergies and emergency contacts, as Apple suggests. Then put a reminder on your own calendar to check the phone for software updates every month or so, since the simplified screen will not tell your relative when one is waiting.
sections.label: Setup Tip

sections.content: Practice a few things together: making a call to a favorite contact, sending a photo, and finding the Emergency keypad. It also helps to explain that the phone is simply showing fewer things for now.

Assistive Access will not suit everyone. If your parent enjoys browsing the web and downloading apps, the full iPhone is probably the better choice. But for someone who mainly wants to call, text and see the grandkids, a calmer screen may make the phone feel friendlier. Take it slowly, ask what they want from the phone, and adjust as you go.

products.name: iPhone 17
products.price: $929 for 256GB unlocked; $1,129 for 512GB unlocked (Apple store price, November 2026); check current price
products.blurb: Suits families buying a new phone who want a 6.3-inch display, with up to 45 hours of video playback by Apple's figure for the base model. Apple advertises trade-in credit of up to $900 and 0% financing.

products.name: iPhone 16
products.price: $829 for 128GB unlocked (Apple store price, November 2026); check current price and confirm at checkout
products.blurb: Suits buyers who want a lower starting price, though that is for 128GB versus the iPhone 17's 256GB, and no full spec list was captured for this model. Apple advertises up to $855 off with an eligible trade-in of an iPhone 8 Plus or newer.
